key_insight: The paper introduces "tensor similarity," a weight-space metric for tensor-based models that determines when two network components implement the same computation by being invariant to weight-space symmetries that break basis-dependent comparisons.
problem_solved: Verifying mechanistic equivalence between parts of neural networks: existing metrics either rely on empirical behaviour (and fail OOD) or compare parameters in a basis-dependent way (ignoring symmetries), preventing reliable matching of implementations.
method: Define a weight-based similarity metric on tensor objects (layers/submodules) that is invariant to canonical weight-space symmetries (e.g., permutations/scalings) relevant to tensor-based models.
Align or quotient out symmetry degrees of freedom between two components, then compute a similarity score comparing their tensor representations rather than only behavioural outputs.
Use the score to identify mechanistic matches across models, enabling comparison even when empirical tests miss out-of-distribution differences.
impact: Provides a principled, symmetry-aware tool for mechanistic interpretability, enabling robust identification and transfer of computations across models and supporting safer, more generalizable interpretive claims.
visual_elements: Schematic of two networks with highlighted subcomponents connected by an arrow labeled "tensor similarity" (showing matching despite different bases)
Illustration of symmetry transformations (permutations/scalings) being factored out before comparison
Heatmap or matrix of similarity scores across many layer pairs to show cluster/group detection of equivalent modules
Workflow infographic: extract tensors → remove symmetries/align → compute similarity → interpret/transfer
paper_title: When Are Two Networks the Same? Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability
paper_authors: ML Nissen Gonzalez, Melwina Albuquerque, Laurence Wroe, Jacob Meyer Cohen, Logan Riggs Smith
